review:
If you have played Dawn of War (2004) and it's expansions, do not expect the large scale battles and base building of the first installation, but rather smaller and micromanagement tactics for multiplayer. The campaign no longer has base building and is replaced with a more tactical RTS with an RPG and weapons and equipment system that allows different builds for different playstyles. The campaign is also playable in co-op which allows for easier micromanagement during gameplay albeit with good coordination and teamwork.

Dawn of War 2 just marked it's 15th anniversary, and received a major update to include Chaos Rising and Retribution and DLC in one package, even though Chaos Rising was included to DoW2 in a previous update. Although it sounds great in theory, it makes the entire package only a bit less expensive than buying them separately before. I applaud Relic Entertainment for updating Dawn of War 1 & 2 because those 2 games and expansions along with Company of Heroes series are the flagship games of Relic, [spoiler] Dawn of War 3 is hated by new and returning players because the developers did not know the core of what players love about DoW 1 & 2. [/spoiler] and everyone who owns the games will receive a free update.

Because Relic updated one of their flagship titles, I hope one day a true DoW 1  and 2 remaster/remake will be released which actually gives long time players what they want. Maybe a proper remake of DoW 3 will be made that actually is faithful to the first 2 games, and perhaps a proper DoW 4.

Hope is the first step in the road to disappointment, but let hope become faith in the Emperor that he will help Relic give the players what they truly want, and restore them to and perhaps go beyond their former glory!

If you looked at this one because of the re-release of the first one then read on because there are changes in this game from the first.

For starters, this game focuses more on hero units than a giant army. In a skirmish, you will most likely have much smaller armies than that of the first one. However, this game took pages from the Men at War game to include better tactics rather than just throw everything you have at the enemy.

Base building has been gutted, for better or worse. Now, you just have an HQ where you can deploy your units. You get power and requisitions from strategic points. So the game rewards you for a more aggressive play rather than defensive. No turtling if that's how you like to play.

There are only 6 playable factions compared to the first game, but in fairness, some of the races played to similarly in my opinion so for better or for worse, there's that.


If you decide to buy the game, you will get the base game, and the two expansions. However, they all have their own launchers, which Dawn of War re-release put it all in one.

For $10, no questions asked take my money for the Emperor. The regular price is too much of an ask. I do not care if that is heresy, it is my opinion.

When Dawn of War II came out, it was an absolutely groundbreaking title. It offered some of the most competitive multiplayer at the time, and the later addition of The Last Stand mode offered hours of entertainment to both casual gamers and pro-players alike.

Now, if in 2015 the size of the multiplayer community has dwindled only to a fraction of what it was, you can still find other players out there (steam forums help in this regard) and enjoy some good games, or just plunge straight through the campaign.

Dawn of War II was worth every cent at the time it was released. As part of a Steam Sale, however, there's no reason for you not to pick this up and give it a go. Especially if you're already  fan of the first Dawn of War, or just appreciate the universe of Warhammer 40,000 in general.

Are you a complete noob to [i]WH40K[/i]? Have you also never played squad based tactical strategy games before? Do you have zero nostalgia for this? Well, I'm happy to tell you none of these things matter. This game is easy to pick up and doesn't feel aged at all. Looks and plays great. The campaign has very "just one more mission" feel to it.

I will say, however, that the campaign can also get grindy and repetitive. You may consider paying the 3€ extra (during sales) to get the [i]Master Collection[/i]. [b]Retribution[/b] is a standalone expansion to this game and allows you to play as more factions than just the space marines. So you may want to start a campaign in both games to keep it fresh. [b]Chaos Rising[/b] is a followup to the main game, so don't start that one at the same time.

[strike] My another little complain is that this game got me interested in WH40K and I ended up buying some short stories* to get some sort of idea what this is all about. Boy did I quickly learn what the term [i]grimdark[/i] means. And then I realized it's really missing from this game. This is a pretty lighthearted game by the franchise's standards. I guess if you want to get some of that grimdark feel, you may want to put some of the WH40K inspired dark ambient music in the background, such as [i]Monasterium Imperi[/i]. Really changes the feel of the game.

* = I started with [b]Sacrifice[/b] by [i]Ben Counter[/i]. Only 28 pages, so it's a quick read and a very good introduction to the vibe of the WH40K universe. [/strike]

[i]Edit: Having read a couple more short stories I realized that Sacrifice was just a very moody (and good) one to start with. These games are actually a very good representation of the WH40k vibe. Also, I quit the main campaign about 2/3 through. Can't take the grind anymore. Jumped straight to CHAOS RISING and it is so much better. [/i]

Warhammer 40,000 Dawn of War II is a fantastic game that blends the best aspects of real-time strategy and role-playing games into one unforgettable experience. As a fan of the original Dawn of War, I was delighted to find an even better game this time around. The graphics are stunning, the gameplay is instinctive and easy to master and the storyline is top-notch.

The game has something for everyone; from strategy gamers to RPG fans. You can choose from four races - Space Marines, Orks, Eldar and Tyranids - and each has a unique set of abilities that will challenge even the most veteran tactician. The real depth of the game is is in the campaign mode, where you lead your chosen race against a variety of enemies from the Warhammer 40,000 universe.

The game also features an online multiplayer mode, where you can take on up to seven opponents in the ongoing struggle to control the galaxy. The tried-and-tested class system means that you can tailor your experience to suit your own play style, while the selection of customisable battlefields provide endless replayability.

All in all, I'd heartily recommend Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War II to anyone who's looking for an innovative and captivating strategy experience. From the gorgeous visuals to the tremendous depth of content, this is one game that lives up to the considerable expectations of the Dawn of War series.

[h3]Aid the mysterious Blood Ravens defeat an Ork Waaagh, the scheming shenanigans of the Eldar and the omni-munching of the Tyranids, all while stealing other (more prominent) chapters' stuff..[/h3]
[u]First and foremost:[/u] This will be a review considering the single player campaign of the game. I did play some multiplayer back in the days, but today I would expect the online games to be few and far in between..

Dawn of War is a natural continuation of the first Dawn of War where the suspiciously well equipped Blood Ravens fought back a chaos uprising while splurting oneliners and breaking all sorts of 40k-canon. This time the main foe is the relentless hive mind of the tyranid swarm that threatens to devour the sector in its unyielding omnivorous streak of galactic domination. However, both the sly and hi-tech Eldar as well as the ferocious battle mushrooms, da Orkz, have shown up in the sector for better and for worse. Who will end up victorious in this swirling battle of domination, and will the mystery of the Blood Ravens finally unravel?

The gameplay is a bit different from the first game in that you control a “hero” type character tied to a specific unit of known space marine formations. For example you have the sneaky scouts, the heavy weapon devastators and the boring but versatile tactical marines. Between missions you level up your main dude as well as equip your units with weapons and armor, tactical orbital bombardments and handgrenades, all to better subdue your foes in the name of the emperor. While on planetside you have your more standardised RTS but with an emphasis on tactical cover and item recovery. The unit's unique abilities and items make the game quite different depending on your choice of skills, yet some enemies require certain abilities to take down efficiently, so choose wisely..   
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3378425989 
Now, the general gist of the game is a positive one, especially if you enjoy RTSes and the grim darkness of the 40k. However, this game can get a bit grindy, especially on the higher difficulties which more or less makes defending objectives pointless. My solution to this would be, play it for the story at a lower difficulty, unless you really love running back and forth across the map to respawn and resupply.. The story is rather cheesy, but not completely without merit. I would love to see a bit more nuance in the space marines since they are more or less all grumpy old men, but then again I am of the notion that the empire is the most boring part of 40k anyways, and yet the most popular by far..

In the end this is a weak but sturdy recommendation. Nowadays you get it all for real cheap during a sale, and honestly with a coop-buddy to take the edge of the otherwise monotonous setting up and tearing down coverfire it is an enjoyable romp across a warridden sector. However, be aware that its solution to difficulty is basically making everything a bullet sponge, and if you find that to be obnoxious, go for an easier difficulty and enjoy mowing down hormagaunts like there is no tomorrow..

As far as WH 40K games go, this game and its associated expansions are basically God-tier. 

First, I want to touch on the overall aesthetic of the game. It does a great job of bringing the WH 40K universe to life in a way that really hadn't been done before its release. Most of the tone is set by the dialogue and over-the-top voice acting (did I mention this game has Steve Blum in it?), which is actually a positive in a sci-fi universe where everything is absurdly overdone. This game really feels like it's being authentic and deferrent to the source material itself rather than just piling in a bunch of references, and it's no coincidence that the Blood Ravens went from being an invention just for this series to one of the most popular space marine chapters in canon.

In gameplay terms, this game is unoriginal, but still very fun. It relies heavily on other the Company of Heroes series, which really shouldn't be a surprise given that both games were produed by Relic and THQ. That's why I can't really fault them for unoriginality in this regard: sure, the gameplay is something you can get elsewhere, but Relic knew what they were doing and they did it well. This reliance on Company of Heroes style combat also gave this game the odd distinction as the only game I can think of in which space marines ACTUALLY USE COVER, which if you're at all familiar with the lore and tabletop game, you know they HAVE to do in order to survive (I know cover got nerfed a bit in 7th edition with widely available 'Ignores Cover,' and I haven't checked much into 8th edition, but I digress).

Anyways, this game gets a solid 9/10, become Force Commander Hair Gel and lead your SPESS MEHREENS to glory today.

If you're looking for incredibly zealous outcries to inspire your daily actions, then this is the game for you. Dawn of War II is the sequel to the original Dawn of War and all its expansions and it delivers in spades. 

For starters, this game is built on the rich lore and backstory of the Warhammer universe. After their disasterous defeat on Kaurava, the Blood Ravens are down to but a single star sytem from where to recruit their new members to fight in the Holy Emperor's name. One problem; the Tyrannids are coming and they have an appetite for planets and everything that lives on it. You control the Force Commander. A nameless, and voiceless avatar who leads a small taskforce from planet to planet to stop the Hive Fleet before it devours the precious planets of the aurelia system. 

Contrary to the original Dawn of War, this game is focussed on tactics rather than strategy and plays out on a much smaller scale. Instead of base building and massing armies you control up to four units, each with their own abilities and weapons. The game also introduces an RPG element that allows you to customise your squads with new armour, weapons and other items to smite the enemies of man. 

It is therefore such a shame that there is only one campaign to play. This game offers four different races to play as, but does not allow you to play them in the same narrative context as the space marines. That said, this game's campaign is no slouch. It is a fully realised story with stellar voice acting accross the board. If brawny men with zealous convictions are not your thing, then you better pass on this pack of awesomeness. Unfortunately for you, there are no other reasons to not get it, so what are you waiting for?

The original review included only the skirmish and the DOW2 campaing in it. After a year, I've finished the DLC campaing Chaos Rising as well so time to update. How is DOW2? How is the skirmish, the campaing and the DLC campaing? Why does DOW2 have both its and its DLCs campaing while DOW2 Chaos Rising still exists as a game on Steam that you can have in your library with a download size of 0 bytes?

+The graphics aren't bad, some stuff looks nice. Cutscenes often looked really good.
+The upgrade system for your units is good. Upgrading their skills and giving them different equipment is very fun. This is expanded upon greatly in the DLC campaing Chaos Rising in which you can give them corrupting, Chaos influenced equipment as well.
+The DLC campaing improves on the game in meaningful ways. The characters get to talk more, show their personalities more. There's more characters and equipment in general. The missions are generally more fun.
+The voice acting at certain points falls short but overall its pretty good. The characters felt generally annoying in the DOW2 campaing but in the DLC campaing I started to enjoy the characters more mainly because they talked more and you could understand them a little better. The DLCs corruption mechanic (which isn't done that well but whatever) makes you use different squads at times which is nice.

-The first campaing sucks without a doubt. It is boring, it is long, overstays it welcome and the gameplay or the story aren't interesting enough to keep me going. I finished it cuz I had to for the review. The last mission was good but getting there sucks.
-The DLC campaing *is* better however its very long as well and overstays it welcome. A lot of the boss battles devolve into "shoot, shoot, oh no our health is low, run away to the closest beacon, lick our wounds, attack again" some of the missions are enjoyable while some others drag on for far too long. You do get more squads, more equipment and even Chaos influenced, corrupting equipment which can effect the endings you get. I got the best ending I could, as pure as I could be in the eyes of the Emperor and it sucked and the game isn't good enough for me to try to get the Chaos ending. While it is better its not enough to actually be good aside from certain segments here and there.
-The skirmish sucks. I'm glad the Tyranids are playable now but the Necrons are gone, the Imperial Guard is gone, the Tau like forget the factions even base building is gone. Yeah, you don't build a base anymore. The skirmish in DOW1 felt more like... a proper skirmish, a match you'd see in other games too like idk Company of Heroes where bases start small, new buildings are added over time and each one builds more powerful and bigger toys at the cost of more supplies and there's buildings just for upgrading units etc. etc. thats the usual "skirmish" you expect right. Its how it is in similar games, its how it is in the first game, I see it as a core identity of DOW but in here its gone and it makes me so sad.
-There's no loss. There's no failure. You have to *try* to fail. In the campaing, you have 4 units and you can deploy them all. In the DLC campaing you have like 7-8 and you can deploy 4 at a time. In both campaings if an units health goes down to 0 they get "knocked out" and can be revived at no cost as long as another unit goes next to them and "revives" them which takes like 30 seconds and costs nothing. There's no death, there's no loss, there's no mission failures... You have to try to fail. Especially when you really equip and upgrade your squads you just become really OP and only bosses (sometimes) are a threat to you but until that point the game is "hit your head against this brick wall, fail, fall back and lick your wounds, try again and eventually you'll win"

You want a good, fun, linear campaing? Try out DOW1. You want a good, fun but more of a dynamic campaing? DOW1 Dark Crusade or Soulstorm is for you. You want fun skirmishes? DOW1 Soulstorm especially with mods is the best you're getting. DOW2 is not worth it and while its DLC, Chaos Rising, is better its not good enough. There is no victory here because failure or "getting close to failing and bringing it back" does not exist. There's no base building, there's just... I don't know. It has its good points, it definitely does but I do not think its anywhere close to how fun DOW1 and its DLCs or expansion packs were.

I don't normally weigh in, but seeing the mixed reviews on this game is prompting me to jump in. DoW II is such a breath of fresh air, if you're expecting a standard 4x type rts you're going to be disappointed. If you come in expecting an rpg flavored squad based (like company of heroes) type game, you're going to really enjoy it. I love the leveling up, gear upgrades, squad selection before missions, the whole game just scratches an itch I never knew I had. One of my top 5 games, for sure. I'm not actually sure why they decided to make this a direct sequel to the first game, as it does not seem to have anything in common with it, nor does it have any of the same mechanics.

This is essentially a RTS-XCOM game, you control a limited number of squads each mission, anywhere from 2-4 I believe, and you go through different sectors/defend them at times. There is the occasional "boss fight" which isn't a traditional boss of any type, just an enemy like all the others really that has a couple special abilities that are very, very easily telegraphed and outmaneuvered. In essence, the boss fights are really just a couple minutes of attacking a boring bullet sponge.

If you're excited about seeing the whole "Play through your chosen race's campaign" part though, don't bother with that either- bit of false advertising that. Not only do you only play as the Space Marines Blood Raven Chapter for the first campaign, but you also only play them for both DLCs. Incredibly, INCREDIBLY disappointing- and very irritating, not to mention awfully boring.

Overall, I can't recommend you purchase this game. For five dollars, if you enjoy games similar to XCOM, I'd go ahead and grab it. But if you're looking for something like a true RTS, or like the first DoW/Starcraft/Supreme Commander, this is NOT the game for you.

Unlike many other RTS games of the time, I genuinely believe that this game has only gotten better with age. 

This game is much slower paced than most other RTS games, allowing me precious moments to read what's happening on the battlefield and react accordingly. Not only that but I do really appreciate the different approach this game offers to how units are managed. The result makes it feel like it's more of a real time tactical strategy game with ARPG elements.

As a fan of both tactics and RPGs as well as RTS in smaller doses, the fusion of those genres that this game offers in it's ambitous campaign mode was and still is a breath of fresh air, perhaps even moreso now than ever before, because like Mechabellum, this is one of the few strategy games that helped me realized I actually do still love this genre, which when compared to games like Starcraft 2 that require a lot of constant multitasking and micromanaging, is greatly appreciated for my aging brain.

"Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War II" is a real-time strategy game set in the grim and expansive universe of Warhammer 40K. With its tactical gameplay, engaging storyline, and immersive universe, it stands as a solid entry in the RTS genre.

Players control a small group of elite units, each with unique abilities and specialties, emphasizing strategy and careful maneuvering over base-building and resource management. The game's multiplayer aspect adds to its longevity, offering competitive matches and cooperative gameplay, allowing players to team up or compete against each other in strategic battles.

However, "Dawn of War II" deviates from traditional RTS gameplay by focusing primarily on tactical combat, which might not appeal to all RTS enthusiasts. The absence of base-building and resource management could be seen as a drawback for players seeking a more traditional RTS experience.

Overall, "Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War II" is a game that I recommend, especially to fans of tactical RTS games and the Warhammer 40K universe. Its emphasis on tactical combat, engaging storyline, and immersive visuals make it a worthwhile experience for those seeking a strategic and atmospheric journey into the grim darkness of the future. While it might not cater to all RTS preferences due to its departure from traditional mechanics, its strengths in tactical gameplay and immersive storytelling make it a solid recommendation for Warhammer and RTS enthusiasts alike.

Fans of the Warhammer universe rejoice! Warhammer 40k: Dawn of War II is the sequel to Dawn of War where the epic tale of the Blood Ravens continues.

Control & Gameplay:
Warhammer 40k: Dawn of War ll renews the Dawn of War genre by adding some new core elements. The well known base building and creation of armies have been replaced by tight squad control, where the micromanagement of these squads will lead to a successful mission. You control each squad's loadout, specialization, abilities and generally everything about them. You will also need to take heed of the terrain, where to take cover, where to move and so on. This might seem as a giant leap away from the first Dawn of War series, and it certainly is. It takes some time to become accustomed with the new game mechanics, but once you get settled, the game is quite enjoyable. In campaign mode, each mission will allow you to choose 4 specialized squads who gain XP and items by completing each mission. There is a fixed number of squads to choose from. In multiplayer, the goal is to capture points and hold them, while building additional squads to supplement your commander in battle. The only building available on the field of battle is the headquarters, from which you can spawn more troops. 

The controls are accurate and function without any trouble. In multiplayer, however, if a player is experiencing lag issues, it will affect the entire match, thus rendering control of your units more difficult or even impossible, if someone has a high latency. However, this issue is not prevalent, at least not from my experience. 

Fun Factor:
Apart from the new style of gameplay, which can be a huge turn off for some players, Dawn of War ll is as original in its story as the previous games. The story remains rich and plays a significant part in the game, as you uncover dark secrets regarding the unknown past of the Blood Ravens. 
Currently, the game is being converted to Steamworks from Games for Windows Live. Therefore, if anyone chooses to buy the game now, beware that large segments of multiplayer is currently unavailable for use.

Graphics & Audio
The visual aspect of the game is a continuation from the previous style: still dark and gritty, but with added details. 
The soundtrack is heavy and it enhances the coarse and gritty quality of the game. For the most part, it supplements the game subliminally. After a while, I did not even notice it due to the constant shooting and blowing up of mines, detonation charges and xeno matter flying around. 

Replayability:
I have spent 100+ hours on this game already, so I would argue that the replayability is indeed high. Even more so with the two expansions: Chaos Rising and Retribution. 
In the original Dawn of War 2, there is a campaign and multiplayer mode. Additionally, the campaign can be played both singleplayer and multiplayer through COOP, which I would highly recommend. 
Furthermore, another mode was introduced, namely "The Last Stand". Here, a group of 3 commandos are pitted against 20 waves of unrelenting xenos. Definitely worth hours of fun and frustration. 

Conclusion:
Despite the fact that Dawn of War ll has moved away from the original Dawn of War games in terms of mechanics, the game still offers exciting gameplay, a well-structed narrative and solid campaign. Where the older games focused on base building and overwhelming your opponent, the new games focus on managing a handful of specialist squads. Terrain, cover and movement patterns play a larger role in succeeding missions.
The game does not run optimally online yet, as the whole net client is being transferred from Games for Windows Live to Steamworks. Therefore, this is the only huge minus about the game, for the time being. This will soon change, and therefore, my rating for this game is positive - 9/10.

[h1]Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War II[/h1]
Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War II is the sequel to the iconic RTS game Dawn of War. We now move to the Blood Raven recruitment sector some time after events of Soulstorm, where together with our team we will clash in battle with the forces of the Tyranids, Orcs, Eldar and Chaos. As Chaos Rising is bundled with the base game, I will review this DLC as well.
[h1]The Plot[/h1]
Pretty standard plot for a Warhammer 40k game. We play here as a unit of the Blood Ravens, and our task is to save the sector from the invasion of the Tyranids and the machinations of the Eldar. The plot is mostly "go there to get that so we can do and achieve something else in the end." And so on until the very end until the final battle. It's a shame we got so little interactions with the Imperial Guard. The beginning of the plot is pretty slow, and for quite a while I had no idea where it was all going, and I got a little put off, but about halfway through the game really kicked off and I was really enjoying myself. A big help here are conversations between our comrades who comment on the current situation and tell stories that develop, improve and complete the threads of Dawn of War 1, and all DLC for that game. Overall it's a strong sequel, every character and every region is well represented and there's always something interesting to look for. The motivations of allies and enemies are understandable, each race has different plans for the final fate of the sector, but it is very accurate with Warhammer lore, so the plot in this game allows you to really get into the universe, although as I said before, there is no greater intrigue here.
[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
A huge change in the formula compared to the previous part of the series. This time, instead of commanding large armies, we now command small teams of soldiers led by the main characters and our companions. We ourselves stand in the shoes of a new commander who is tasked with solving the issue of the anarchy in the sector. He has no name or voice, but since he looks like Vanilla Ice, I will simply call him "VI". VI and the rest of our companions show the latest mechanics of this game, i.e. the system in which we develop the skills of our characters, and give them a ton of new equipment. And yes, I know we could do that in the previous game as well, but it's more personal here, and we have a huge influence on how the characters will behave on the battlefield. It's a bit of a shame that VI didn't get a voice here, because the mute commander of the Space Marine squad is as charismatic as toilet paper, which is a bit odd when you consider that this is a game that relies heavily on tactics and command skills. Because it all boils down to the fact that from the big battles, we are now moving to smaller maps where good placement of units, use of structures, use of cover, skills, etc. is of great importance. At first I wasn't sure about the changes that were going on here, but in the end I really enjoyed them, and while I still prefer Dawn of War 1, this game does a really good job with the mechanics it set out to establish. The campaign map is really well done, we mostly fly from planet to planet and these are really diverse and interesting, although it still doesn't save the game from map repetition. Anyway, the variety in all this is so big that it doesn't bug me so much. What bugs me a lot though are the bosses. I know what they wanted to do here, but apart from the original look, every boss behaves the same, and they are just big, walking damage sponges.
[h1]Chaos Rising[/h1]
DLC that allows us to face the forces of Chaos. It's worth noting here that many of the core systems have been tweaked slightly so everything works a bit better. The conversations between the characters are even better than in the base game, and depending on how we play, these dialogues may be different. I'm talking about the new Chaos corruption system. Depending on our equipment and actions on the battle maps, our team can slowly squad to Chaos, slightly changing their dialogues, and giving us new abilities. It's a tempting option, but it doesn't change the plot much, so it doesn't really matter in the end. Either way, it's a good and thematic detail. And this time we have an intrigue here, and it's quite interesting. The main plot outside of Chaos is our chapter's disintegration through internal betrayal and corruption, and throughout the DLC we discover the magnitude of these phenomena. Compared to the base game, this is a gigantic improvement in storytelling. In addition, we get some original locations, and some cool equipment. Unfortunately, VI is still a blank slate, but here at least they gave us the option to ask questions and give answers to pre-mission dialogues, so VI at least shows some signs of life. And of course, the greater influence of the Imperial Guard in the game is a plus. The only thing I don't like here is the returning Chaos Champion from DoW1, Eliphas. I'm talking about his voice here, because as a character, he's a really great opponent. However, a big part of his charisma in DoW1 was his thick, rumbling voice, and here he sounds like he spent his vacation being kicked in the balls by Slaanesh's followers. Maybe the Chaos Gods cut off his balls and took his helmet as a punishment for failing in the Dark Crusade campaign. But in the end, I wouldn't be surprised at all, it's Warhammer 40k after all.
[h1]Technical Matters[/h1]
Graphically, the game has aged very well, it runs smoothly and does not crash to the desktop. The music is phenomenal, in my opinion it has the best soundtrack in the DoW series. The visual and sound effects are great, you can really influence the environment in a very epic way, and I like the detail that some enemy units don't have wooden death animations and instead turn into Garry's Mod ragdolls when they die so you can admire the jelly bodies of the enemies flying and bouncing around the battlefield. And of course, every voice actor did a brilliant job here, everyone gave it their best, and it shows.
[h1]Summary[/h1]
A game that, despite the great risks it took, tried to do something original, and it succeeded, and despite a few problems, it is a great sequel and continuation of the series. And even though it's a very different game from its predecessor, it's definitely a great classic, and I think it's an appropriate end to the series for now, because I don't acknowledge this thing called DoW3. Maybe someday the series will return to its glory days, and perhaps, with the blessing of the God Emperor, this dream will finally come true one day.

The campaign starts out fine , and the story and world building is good. Each faction with its own motive and direction. Secrets , intrigue , all the sort.

The first crack to the fun experience comes in the repetitive maps. The same maps are used for mutliple missions. The excuse is different factions took the territory and you can capture a secondary building to give you a boost - only one per mission is permitted apparently. 

The second crack is the way they ramp up the challenge. Enemy bosses become bullet sponges. They don't have an interesting attack you have to dodge or a special ability they just have an insane pool of hit points which makes an already tedious affair more tedious.

The final crack and nail in the coffin is the diffculty in the latter half of the campaign. They decided to give all enemies a base , protected by towers. Ok , so far just a harder challenge - no issue . BUT . These bases spawn an infinite amount of units , until you destroy their structures. And this is where the game falls apart for me. You can;t think of a clever way around the enemy since the enemy swarms you from all sides constantly . And after you barely finished a wave another one shows up . Your supplies are limited , the enemies are not.

Overall , i wanted to say the campaign was decent , then mediocre , but by the end it's just a badly designed mess.
Again the skirmish and multiplayer is ok and functional. There are several races to choose form with asymetric play due to different unit types and leaders. Just don;t hold up hope for the campaign being decent.

Pros: 
-It really has great graphics
-You get a sense of "feel" since when playing the campaign. The game somehow managed to let me feel the "hopelesness" when dealing with the tyranid swarm and havingt to deal with the chaos.
-The overall campaign is nice
-Fights between your units and the enemy's are really cool, props to the SFX and level design.

Cons:
-At one point, it became a rinse and repeat "point and click" game where your units go to an area, you manage them, then use as much skills as possible to keep them alive. 
-I don't understand the concept of the "cover" system. I mean, unlike Men of War Assault Squad 2, you have to manually assign each unit to a cover, and even then, the units won't automatically spread out in the cover you chose. Minor thing, but it got annoying at one point.

In conclusion, it's a great game, but it should be its own franchise and not part of the "Dawn of War" series. DoW1 was the embodiment of epicness in the series. I lowered my hopes when I first bought this (on sale) due to the reviews, but this isn't DoW, this is a new category of DoW alongside DoW 3. The disappointing part was, I thought this was a remaster of DoW1.

PS. They should just remaster DoW1, add a campaign for all (major) races, and add in titan class units (and not rely on mods).

It's a masterpiece of an era that loved games as much as we do.

If you liked the original Dawn of War games then this is not for you. They have completely removed the RTS style of the game, no longer do you build your base and push through objectives. You merely start with a hero unit and sometimes a few other units that you can upgrade prior to starting missions.

While this may be enjoyable for some I feel it takes away the original play style of the game thus ruining it for myself.

The old DoW was a basebuilding RTS game ala Starcraft, and it was FANTASTIC... this is NOT the same game, however, it is very in it's own right. Almost all the negative reviews are due to the fact that the core game mechanics have changed, and in my opinion, these negative reviews would likely not have even cropped up had the title of the game been something other than Dawn of War. Being a sequal, people expected more of the same with a few enhancements, instead they got something totally different. 

Pros:
- Decent Graphics for a RTS even today... the animations are a lot of fun.
- Great Micro gaming! If you are into Microing your units in RTS games, that is what the focus of this game is. You can pull off some really cool combos and tactics in this game, especially given all the different types of gear you can combine with various skills.
- The game is fast paced, bloody, and ultra-violent. It IS true to the name WARHAMMER. 
- There RPG aspect of the game is pulled off very well, swapping up your team with various skills and loadouts really changes the gameplay. It's very fun to try new tactics and ideas.
- The star map and mission selection is cool. Sometimes you will have to pass up on a mission to persue a different one and there are reprecussions for your actions. Let a territory fall and you may lose some of your orbital support in the sector, but maybe it was worth it to get that blue legendary reward from the other mission. You can always comeback and reclaim the territory later with bigger better gear. 
- The balancing seems pretty great. For every unit there is a counter, this includes bosses. Take heed to the tips before the missions as they will potentially let you know an enemy's weakness, or give you reports as to what the enemy is bringing to the fight so you can adjust your loadout appropriately. 
- You feel like you are getting stronger throughout the game, and some of the end-game weapons and skills are great!
- Multiplayer is a lot of fun- reminds me of some of the greates Starcraft1 RPG mods.
- A ton of content. I haven't even touched anything other than the base campaign, and then I get to play Chaos... after that if I'm still binging on the game Ill check out the DLC, but you get a LOT of content with just the base game. 

Cons
- Towards the end of the campaign the game begins to get a bit repetitive. 
- Same maps are reused a bit too much. The maps are great, wish they had more.
- Sometimes the pathfinding will drive you insane. Multiple times Ive lost a team because I told them to fall back, and they do so by charging straight into the enemy to go around the long way. Very irritating sometimes. 
- Level Cap at level 20 seems to come a bit soon... I want to keep progressing my heroes!
- The inventory screen could use some filters. Things tend to get a bit muddled and cluttered as you collect more gear. Also, while the character screen shows base stats, it would be nice if it displayed other bonuses given by your equipment (resistances mainly... many different pieces of equipment will boost resistences, but you can only see this when you hover over the items).
- Some of the bosses are kinda lame, while others are pretty awesome with their own unique tactics which can take you by surprise at first. 
- Multiplayer is dying out. hopefully there will be a greater player base with the announcement of DoWIII

I think using the systems built here they have a great formula, and perhaps a different Warhammer franchise of games altogether. I'd love to see the same mechanics expanded upon in another game... BUUUT I also want to see another PROPER sequal to DoW. I enjoy both in their own ways. 

So, looking at the game in a different lens of NOT a base building RTS, but a tactical squad command game, I would highly recommend it 8/10.

This game and its expansions are really great games, a little hard to learn at the start, since it doesn't works like a normal RTS, so it will take some time to click, but when it does, is a glorious fest of battle and blood, just like the Emperor intended. The overall feel seems much different and has a very slow feel to it, even though it's going for fast paced.

Now I'm not the only one that feels this way, one of my friends feels the exact same, and he wishes the game was more like DoW 1. We where hyped that DoW III had base building but that didn't work out to well either.

I feel kind of alone In this situation because everyone (besides me and said friend) seems to like it. So the point of this is if you're like me and just wanted more of what DoW 1 had to offer, don't buy it. if you don't expect the orignal and you want it for the lore and universe, buy it, you'll probobly enjoy it..
